source_url_note: Inferred from post slug in the page's edit link (content/inside-rust/rust-langrust-is-adopting-an-llm-policy.md) and date; no canonical tag in the HTML.

options.label: No policy / status quo
options.description: Keep the 'wild west' approach: unofficial, unpublished moderation notes; 'anything goes, as long as it's not obviously horrible'.

options.label: Total ban
options.description: Ban LLMs altogether: 'No LLM-generated content, whether it be code or prose.'

options.label: Permissive / tool-neutral
options.description: Allow any LLM use considered pro-social: 'AI is a tool, just like other tools we use'.

options.label: Public, written, restrictive-but-scoped policy (adopted)
options.description: Published policy for rust-lang/rust: LLMs fine to answer questions, analyze, distill, refine, check, suggest, review, but not to create; mandatory disclosure; LLM-generated code heavily restricted and held to a higher bar.

cruxes.statement: Polished, well-tested PRs no longer reliably signal the author's effort, understanding, presence, or long-term commitment, undermining norms built on those signals.
cruxes.source: Section 'Technical products no longer indicate effort': 'With LLMs, none of these signals are reliable.'

cruxes.statement: LLMs make code cheaper to write, worsening the existing shortage of review bandwidth, since review is mostly decision-making rather than bug-catching.
cruxes.source: Section 'Making code easier to write causes review issues': 'reviewing is made of decisions'.

cruxes.statement: Mechanically relaying review comments to and from an LLM wastes reviewers' time and breaches the trust that a real person is engaged.
cruxes.source: Section 'Mechanically copy-pasting LLM output is a waste of time': 'We want to hear your thoughts, not a machine's.'

cruxes.statement: Unpublished, inconsistently enforced moderation rules conflict with being transparent and welcoming, because newcomers cannot know the rules.
cruxes.source: Sections 'Why was this policy created?' / 'So why a policy?': 'our rules were not published anywhere'.

cruxes.statement: LLMs can no longer be ignored, so the real choice is between unofficial moderation notes and a policy stood by publicly, not between policy and no policy.
cruxes.source: Section 'So why a policy?': 'Our choices are not "no policy" or "policy".'

cruxes.statement: Rust governs by consensus with no benevolent dictator, and there is no (and likely never will be) consensus on acceptable AI use, ruling out either extreme.
cruxes.source: Section 'So why a policy?': 'Rust governance doesn't work that way.'

cruxes.statement: Some LLM uses genuinely respect the community (translation, finding poor diagnostics, analyzing RFCs), so not all use should be barred.
cruxes.source: Section 'Why was this policy created?': 'Some of those uses respected our community'.

cruxes.statement: Shared values of building deep experts and maintaining an inclusive community ground a focus on human understanding rather than mere working artifacts.
cruxes.source: Sections 'So why a policy?' / 'General rules': 'the policy focuses on understanding'; 'No programmer tapes.'

cruxes.statement: A bright-line disclosure rule lets moderators judge violations by actions rather than intent, even if some parts are unenforceable.
cruxes.source: Section 'Moderation rules': 'The goal is not to catch every violation'.

cruxes.statement: The policy should remain changeable and gather data on LLM contributions, since its rules are imperfect and a disliked written policy pushes governance improvement.
cruxes.source: Sections 'So why a policy?' / 'What next?': 'writing our rules down is better than not writing them down'.

cruxes.statement: Contributors should not be harassed or accused over suspected LLM use, and the burden of disclosing LLM generation lies with the author, not reviewers.
cruxes.source: Sections 'Moderation rules' / 'Reviewers': 'Style is not evidence; please do not accuse people'.

decision.summary: Five Rust teams adopted a public LLM policy for the rust-lang/rust monorepo only (not an official project-wide stance on LLMs).
key_provisions: LLMs fine to answer questions, analyze, distill, refine, check, suggest, review; not to create.
Disclosure required for public LLM content (machine translation, trivial changes, bug discovery, reviewing others' work); private use without disclosure is fine.

LLM-generated code allowed only if pre-arranged, non-critical, high-quality, well-tested, well-reviewed, with disclosure; tests mandatory; soundness-critical changes barred unless author is a domain expert (still strongly discouraged); docs and diagnostics are disallowed areas.
No one required to read LLM output or review LLM PRs; LLM review cannot substitute for human review.
Reviewers may close non-compliant PRs with no questions asked, pointing to #llm-mentoring; doubtful cases reported privately to moderation.
Provisions make the policy easier to change; leadership council considering an LLM-policy sub-team.

decisive.why: Framed the choice as unofficial notes versus a public policy, making a written public policy the answer.
Transparency and welcoming newcomers motivated formalizing the hidden rules publicly.
Consensus governance and lack of agreement ruled out both a full ban and a permissive stance.
Primary harm (loss of effort/understanding signal) motivating strict restrictions on LLM-created content.
Review-bandwidth burden motivating restrictions and reviewer opt-out.
Copy-paste harm motivating the disclosure and no-unmarked-LLM-comments rules.
